## Strong exogeneity and the CEF

::: {.hidden}
\gdef\E#1{\mathrm{E}\left[#1\right]}
\gdef\Var#1{\mathrm{Var}\left(#1\right)}
\gdef\Cov#1{\mathrm{Cov}\left(#1\right)}
:::

- Consider the linear regression model
  $$
  Y_{i}=\beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}+U_{i}.
  $$

- When the errors are **strongly exogenous**, i.e., $\E{U_{i} \mid X_{i}} = 0$, the linear regression model defines the **CEF** of $Y$ conditional on $X$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CEF}_{Y}\left( X_{i}\right) &\equiv \E{Y_{i} \mid X_{i}} \\
&= \E{\beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}+U_{i} \mid X_{i}} \\
&= \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}+\E{U_{i} \mid X_{i}} \\
&= \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Weak exogeneity

- Consider the linear regression model with $\E{U_{i}} = 0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{i} &= \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}+U_{i}, \\
\E{U_{i}} &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

- Suppose the errors are only **weakly exogenous**:
  $$
  \E{U_{i}X_{i}} = 0.
  $$

- In this case,
  $$
  \mathrm{CEF}_{Y}\left( X_{i}\right) \neq \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}.
  $$

- **Question:** What does the econometrician estimate when running a linear regression and the regressors are *not* strongly exogenous?

## Misspecified CEF and the regression error

- Suppose that
  $$
  \E{Y_{i} \mid X_{i}} = g\left( X_{i}\right),
  $$
  where $g$ is some unknown *nonlinear* function. Thus, the **true** CEF is $g\left( X_{i}\right) \neq \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}.$

- Define $V_{i}=Y_{i}-\E{Y_{i} \mid X_{i}}$, so the true model is $Y_{i} = g\left( X_{i}\right) +V_{i}$ with $\E{V_{i} \mid X_{i}} = 0$.

- Adding and subtracting $\beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{i} &= g\left( X_{i}\right) +V_{i} \\
&= \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}-\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) +V_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

- Rearranging, $Y_{i}=\beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}+U_{i}$, where
  $$
  U_{i}=V_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}.
  $$

- Can we find $\beta _{0}$ and $\beta _{1}$ so that $\E{U_{i}} = 0$ and $\E{X_{i}U_{i}} = 0$? If yes, how can we interpret such $\beta _{0}$ and $\beta _{1}$?

## Conditions for weak exogeneity

$$
U_{i}=V_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}.
$$

- Evaluating $\E{U_i}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{U_{i}}
&= \E{V_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}} \\
&= \E{V_{i}}+\E{g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}} \\
&= \E{g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}},
\end{aligned}
$$

- For the covariance condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{U_{i}X_{i}}
&= \E{\left( V_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) X_{i}} \\
&= \E{V_{i}X_{i}}+\E{\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) X_{i}} \\
&= \E{\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) X_{i}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Thus, to have $\E{U_{i}} = \E{U_{i}X_{i}} = 0$, we need to find $\beta _{0}$ and $\beta _{1}$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}} &= 0, \\
\E{\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) X_{i}} &= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Linear approximation of the CEF

- Consider the following approximation problem:
  $$
  \min_{b_{0},b_{1}}\E{\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -b_{0}-b_{1}X_{i}\right) ^{2}}.
  $$

- We are approximating the CEF with a linear function.

- Among the linear functions, we are looking for the **best** linear approximation in the **mean squared error (MSE)** sense.

## Regression as best linear approximation

- Let $\left( \beta _{0},\beta _{1}\right) =\arg \min_{b_{0},b_{1}}\text{MSE}\left( b_{0},b_{1}\right)$, where $\text{MSE}\left( b_{0},b_{1}\right) =\E{\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -b_{0}-b_{1}X_{i}\right) ^{2}}.$

- The first-order conditions are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial b_{0}} &= -2\E{g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}} = 0, \\
\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial b_{1}} &= -2\E{\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) X_{i}} = 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

- These are the conditions for weak exogeneity derived earlier, so
  $$
  \E{U_{i}} = 0\text{ and }\E{U_{i}X_{i}} = 0.
  $$

- Thus, the linear regression model gives us the best linear approximation of the CEF (in the MSE sense).

## Misspecification and heteroskedasticity

- We have
  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  Y_{i} &= \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}+U_{i}, \\
  U_{i} &= V_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- Suppose that the "true" error $V_{i}$ is homoskedastic: $\E{V_{i}^{2} \mid X_{i}} = \sigma _{V}^{2}$ for all $X_{i}.$

- $U_{i}$ is **heteroskedastic** if $g\left( X_{i}\right) \neq \beta _{0}+\beta _{1}X_{i}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{U_{i}^{2} \mid X_{i}}
&= \E{\left( V_{i}+g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) ^{2} \mid X_{i}} \\
&= \E{V_{i}^{2}+\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) ^{2} \mid X_{i}} \\
&\quad + \E{2V_{i}\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) \mid X_{i}} \\
&= \sigma _{V}^{2}+\left( g\left( X_{i}\right) -\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}X_{i}\right) ^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
